title: Session 4: Conjunctive Adverbs
summary: The most common conjunctive adverbs — however, therefore, moreover, furthermore, in addition, as a result, consequently, nevertheless, on the other hand, for example, instead, otherwise — when to use a semicolon, a full stop or commas with them, and a full review of all four types of conjunctions.

blocks.title: By the end of this session you can …
items: Use the common conjunctive adverbs with the right meaning
Punctuate them correctly: IC; however, IC · IC. However, IC · IC, however, IC
Never join two independent clauses with a comma + however (comma splice)
Choose between all four types of conjunctions to say the same idea in different ways

blocks.text: A **conjunctive adverb** (also called a **linking adverb** or **transition**) shows how two ideas are related — just like a conjunction. But grammatically it is an **adverb**, not a real conjunction, so **it cannot join two independent clauses with a comma**. You need a **semicolon** or a **full stop**.

rows: The flat is cheap. **Moreover**, it is close to the university.
however, nevertheless, on the other hand, in contrast
The plan was good; **however**, it was too expensive.
therefore, as a result, consequently, thus
He missed the bus; **as a result**, he was late.
Some animals sleep all winter; **for example**, bears hibernate.
He didn't take the bus; **instead**, he walked.
Mix the flour and water; **then**, add the eggs.
Cars pollute the air. **Similarly**, factories release harmful gases.
The test was not easy. **In fact**, it was very difficult.

blocks.title: HOWEVER / NEVERTHELESS = contrast
items: However = but: The phone is expensive; **however**, it is very reliable.
Nevertheless = but still (despite this): The weather was terrible; **nevertheless**, the race went ahead.

blocks.title: THEREFORE / AS A RESULT / CONSEQUENTLY = result
items: The roads were icy; **therefore**, the schools closed.
As a result and consequently mean the same. Use them to vary your writing.

blocks.title: MOREOVER / FURTHERMORE / IN ADDITION = addition
items: Use them to add a **new, stronger** point: Exercise improves health. **Furthermore**, it reduces stress.
In addition is the most neutral. Don't put moreover in front of every sentence.

blocks.title: ON THE OTHER HAND / IN CONTRAST = comparing two sides
items: Living in the city is exciting. **On the other hand**, it can be very expensive.
On the other hand is perfect for discussion and argument essays (one side → other side).

blocks.title: FOR EXAMPLE / FOR INSTANCE = giving an example
items: Many foods are high in sugar; **for example**, fizzy drinks contain up to ten teaspoons a can.
Use them to support a point with evidence in a paragraph.

blocks.title: INSTEAD / OTHERWISE
items: Instead = in place of that: She didn't go to the party; **instead**, she stayed home and studied.
Otherwise = if not: Save your work regularly; **otherwise**, you may lose it.

rows: The test was hard**; however,** everyone passed.
The test was hard**. However,** everyone passed.
**at the end of a clause** (less common)

blocks.title: The most common mistake: comma + however
items: ✗ The test was hard, however everyone passed. → This is a **comma splice** (two ICs joined by a comma only).
✓ The test was hard; however, everyone passed.
✓ The test was hard. However, everyone passed.
✓ The test was hard, but everyone passed. (FANBOYS can join with a comma — however cannot.)

blocks.title: Sentence starters: always a comma after them
items: When a conjunctive adverb or a time/sequence word starts a sentence, put a comma after it: **Firstly,** … **Moreover,** … **As a result,** … **Finally,** …

blocks.title: Semicolon or full stop?
items: Use a **semicolon** when the two clauses are closely related and you want one sentence.
Use a **full stop** to start a new sentence. Both are correct; mix them in your writing.

rows: The museum was crowded, **but** we enjoyed the visit.
**Although** the museum was crowded, we enjoyed the visit.
We enjoyed the visit **although** the museum was crowded.
The museum was crowded**; however,** we enjoyed the visit.
The museum was **not only** crowded **but also** very noisy.

items.q: Choose: The road was blocked; ___, we took another route. (however / therefore)
Choose: He was ill; ___, he came to school. (nevertheless / moreover)
Choose: Recycling saves energy. ___, it reduces waste. (Furthermore / Instead)
Choose: Hurry up; ___, we'll be late. (otherwise / for example)
Punctuate: The flight was delayed however we arrived on time
items.a: The flight was delayed; however, we arrived on time. (or: … delayed. However, we …)

items.q: Punctuate: The flight however was delayed
Correct: I studied all night, therefore I passed.
items.a: I studied all night; therefore, I passed.

items.q: Correct: The hotel was cheap but however it was dirty.
items.a: The hotel was cheap, but it was dirty. / The hotel was cheap; however, it was dirty.

items.q: Write the idea in four structures: It was expensive. We bought it.
items.a: It was expensive, but we bought it. · Although it was expensive, we bought it. · We bought it although it was expensive. · It was expensive; however, we bought it.

blocks.title: Session 4 Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 15 questions. Choose the best answer. You see your score and the explanations at the end.

c: It was late however, we stayed.
It was late, however we stayed.
It was late; however, we stayed.
It was late; however we, stayed.
The bus was late. Therefore, I walked.
The bus was late, therefore I walked.
The bus was late, so I walked.
The bus was late; therefore, I walked.

questions.q: He trained every day; ___, he won the competition.
Fast food is cheap. ___, it is often unhealthy.
Smoking damages the lungs. ___, it increases the risk of heart disease.
Many sports are good for the heart; ___, swimming and cycling.
Wear your coat; ___, you will catch a cold.
She didn't watch TV; ___, she read a book.

c: The students; however, were not happy.
The students, however were not happy.
The students however, were not happy.
The students, however, were not happy.

questions.q: Which word can join two ICs with **only a comma** before it?
The storm was terrible; ___, nobody was hurt.
Which sentence means the same as Although it rained, we played?
c: It rained; for example, we played.
The plan was good however; it failed.
The plan was good; but, it failed.
The plan was good; however, it failed.
The plan was good, but however it failed.
